metaTitle: Arizona Property Tax Appeal Demand Letter | Over-Assessment
metaDescription: Generate an Arizona over-assessed property value challenge demand letter. Cite A.R.S. § 42-16051, meet deadlines, and protect your right to appeal.
statuteCitation: A.R.S. § 42-16051 (Petition for Review of Valuation) and § 42-16201 (Appeal to Court)

introParagraph: If you own property in Arizona and believe your county assessor has overvalued it, state law gives you a clear—but time-sensitive—right to challenge the assessment. Each year the assessor mails a Notice of Value listing the property's full cash value (FCV) and limited property value (LPV). These figures directly drive your tax bill. Arizona law allows owners to dispute an inflated valuation administratively with the assessor, then with the State or County Board of Equalization, and ultimately in Tax Court. A well-drafted demand letter, sent before deadlines expire, often resolves the dispute without litigation. This page explains Arizona's appeal framework, the strict 60-day window, and how a written challenge letter can compel the assessor to correct an over-assessment and refund excess taxes.
lawExplanation: Arizona property is valued annually by the county assessor under A.R.S. Title 42. The assessor determines the property's full cash value (FCV) and its limited property value (LPV); the limited property value is the prior year's limited value plus five percent, and it cannot exceed full cash value (A.R.S. § 42-13301). The assessor notifies each owner of both values on a date before March 1 (A.R.S. § 42-15101). Under A.R.S. § 42-16051, an owner who disagrees may file a petition with the assessor, on the prescribed form, within sixty days after the notice of valuation is mailed. If the assessor denies relief, A.R.S. § 42-16056 allows an appeal within twenty-five days after the decision is mailed, to the county board of equalization (or the state board where no county board exists) or to superior court. An owner may also appeal directly to court on or before December 15 without exhausting administrative remedies, or within sixty days after the most recent administrative decision on a petition (A.R.S. § 42-16201). If the court finds excessive valuation, it enters judgment for the excess taxes plus costs (A.R.S. § 42-16213), and the county treasurer pays the judgment with interest at the legal rate on the overpayment (A.R.S. § 42-16214). Owner-occupied residential property is class three (A.R.S. § 42-12003), so a classification error is also a ground to challenge.
letterStrategy: A demand letter to the county assessor is often the fastest, lowest-cost way to fix an Arizona over-assessment. The letter should identify the parcel by APN, reference the Notice of Value date and amount, and state clearly that you are filing a petition under A.R.S. § 42-16051. Include your opinion of value and supporting evidence: recent comparable sales in the same neighborhood, a fee appraisal, photos of deferred maintenance or damage, vacancy data for income property, or documentation of an incorrect classification. Show that you are timely by citing the sixty days from the date the notice was mailed, and reserve your right to appeal further if the assessor refuses to correct the value. The letter creates a written record, and if the assessor denies the petition, the same evidence transfers into your board petition or court complaint.
proceduralNotes: Under A.R.S. § 12-172, a taxpayer may elect small claims procedures in the tax court for class three property or where the full cash value is two million dollars or less (valuation disputes). The tax court is the tax department of the superior court in Maricopa County (A.R.S. § 12-161). Deadlines matter: the sixty-day petition window and the December 15 direct-appeal date come from the statutes cited above. Taxes for the year under appeal must be paid before delinquency or the court dismisses the appeal, with two exceptions (A.R.S. § 42-16210). Consult the Arizona Department of Revenue and your county assessor's website for current forms.

faq.q: How do I know if my Arizona property is over-assessed?
faq.a: Compare the full cash value on your Notice of Value to recent sale prices of similar properties in your neighborhood. If comparable homes have sold for materially less than your full cash value, or if your property has unrepaired damage, functional issues, or was misclassified, you likely have grounds. A licensed appraisal or a Realtor's comparative market analysis strengthens the challenge.

faq.q: What is the deadline to challenge an Arizona property assessment?
faq.a: You may file a petition with the county assessor under A.R.S. § 42-16051 within sixty days after the notice of valuation is mailed. Alternatively, under A.R.S. § 42-16201 you may appeal directly to court on or before December 15, or within sixty days after the most recent administrative decision on your petition. Confirm the dates on your own notice.

faq.q: Do I have to pay property taxes while appealing?
faq.a: Generally yes. Under A.R.S. § 42-16210, taxes for the year under appeal must be paid before delinquency or the court dismisses the appeal, with two exceptions. If the court finds the valuation excessive, it enters judgment for the excess taxes plus costs under A.R.S. § 42-16213.

faq.q: Can I file in Arizona small claims tax court?
faq.a: A taxpayer may elect small claims procedures under A.R.S. § 12-172 for class three property or where the full cash value of the property is two million dollars or less. The election is made by captioning the complaint as a small claims procedure in the tax court.

faq.q: What evidence works best in an Arizona valuation appeal?
faq.a: Recent arm's-length comparable sales of similar properties in the same neighborhood are the usual starting point, and a licensed appraisal adds weight. For commercial property, income and expense statements supporting an income approach help. Photos documenting damage, deferred maintenance, or functional obsolescence also help, as do records showing classification errors.
